See Agentic Performance Management on Your Books

Finance teams have spent years layering point solutions on top of an ERP: close management tools that coordinate people, consolidation software that reports after the fact, and copilots that answer questions without acting on them. None of these execute the underlying accounting work. Agentic Performance Management closes that gap.

APM describes a coordinated system of specialized agents that operates on top of an existing ERP to independently complete multi-step accounting workflows, with traceability and human oversight built in.

Rather than assisting a person through reconciliation, consolidation, or flux analysis, the agents perform the work directly and escalate only genuine exceptions for review. The result is a system that acts on the books rather than one that only describes them.

This distinction matters because the categories APM gets compared to (ERP, EPM, RPA, and AI copilots) all play a different role in the accounting stack. Each is covered in more depth further down this page.

The Four Core Principles of APM
Four principles define what separates Agentic Performance from every adjacent category of tool.

Agents complete accounting workflows rather than recommend a next step for someone else to take. Controllers and finance leaders shift from doing the work to reviewing it, reserving judgment for the decisions that actually need it.

APM treats "done" as a daily state rather than a month-end milestone. Agents validate, reconcile, and keep the books ready for close in near real time, which cuts down the scramble that typically defines the final days of a period.
The platform works across multiple ERPs, entities, and currencies without a system migration, functioning as a control layer that unifies fragmented structures rather than replacing them.
Every action runs inside rules, thresholds, and approval paths defined in natural language. Teams decide when escalation is required and can access full documentation at any time.

How APM Compares to ERP, EPM, RPA, and AI Copilots

Agentic Performance Management gets compared to categories it isn't, from the ERP that records transactions and the EPM platform that plans against that data, to RPA scripts that follow fixed rules without judgment and AI copilots that draft answers for a person to act on.

This approach operates on top of all of these, executing the accounting work that would otherwise require direct human involvement, with logics and learning mechanisms that adapt to how an entity's books actually behave.

An ERP serves as the system of record, and an EPM platform plans against that record once it has been cleaned up. Agentic Performance Management sits between the two, executing the reconciliation and consolidation work that determines whether the data reaching EPM can actually be trusted, a distinction unpacked in

Business process management tools coordinate workflow across a team, and enterprise performance management tools plan and forecast against whatever numbers they're handed, but neither one executes the underlying accounting work the way these agents do, a gap laid out in

Close management software digitizes checklists and tracks who owns each task, yet a person still has to complete the work behind every line item on that list. This platform replaces the coordination layer with execution, since agents run the matching, reconciliation, and flux work the checklist was only ever tracking, the full comparison covered in
APM vs. Close Management Tools and EPM
The clearest way to separate true APM from a tool that only sounds agentic is to ask a few direct questions during evaluation:
•  Does the tool complete workflows end to end, or does it only produce suggestions for someone else to act on?
•  Can it write back to the general ledger, or does it stop at a recommendation?
•  Does it run continuously, or only at close?
•  Are approval thresholds and escalation rules explicit, or is governance unclear?
•  Is there a full audit trail with transaction-level support behind every number?
•  Does it work across existing ERPs without requiring a migration?
A platform that can't answer all six clearly is likely a rules engine or a coordination layer wearing agentic language, not Agentic Performance Management.

Built for Governance, Not Just Execution

Execution alone doesn't guarantee control, which is why every agent operates inside a defined set of rules: discrepancy thresholds, approval workflows, and escalation paths configured in natural language rather than custom code.

Every action carries documentation and a complete audit trail, and the underlying architecture is designed to support SOC 1 controls. Human reviewers can approve, reject, or refine any result, keeping accountability with the team even as agents take on the execution.
